Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old carpenter and father, heard gunfire while driving home, pursued the gunman into the school, and killed him. Oregon Governor Tina Kotek credited Giamanco with having "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life."

Law enforcement sources said the pump-action shotgun was purchased by Griffin's mother around August. Oregon law generally prohibits minors from possessing firearms, though exceptions exist for certain lawful uses.

Five-Year-Old Rhoam Summer was identified as one of the four victims mourned by families and residents. A 7-year-old child and another teacher remain hospitalized with critical injuries from the shooting.

summary: On Thursday, a 16-year-old gunman forced entry into Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, killing three children ages 5, 8, and 11, plus one teacher, before dying inside, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.

Officers arrived at the campus at 1:02 p.m., minutes after dispatchers received reports of a shooter firing into a car outside the school. An armed community member who witnessed the suspect enter pursued him inside and shot him, authorities said.

Two additional victims—a seven-year-old student and a 54-year-old teacher—remain hospitalized with critical injuries. The attack triggered an immediate facility-wide lockdown, with adjacent campuses also placed under precautionary lockdown.

Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook canceled classes districtwide Friday, while police directed families to Journey Church at 61303 S Highway 97 for reunification with students evacuated by bus.

Oregon Governor Tina Kotek praised the community member's intervention, saying the bystander's actions carry "a heavy emotional burden." The shooting marks the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year, according to a database maintained by The Associated Press and USA Today.
title: 4 Killed, Including 3 Children, in Oregon Elementary School Shooting; Suspect Also Dead

summary: President Donald Trump announced Thursday that the Pentagon will not livestream the firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, reversing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's plan to broadcast the event online.
Growing public opposition prompted the reversal, as Hegseth had originally proposed streaming the December 3 execution by firing squad to demonstrate America's response to terrorism.
Hasan, a former Army Major, killed 13 people and injured 32 in a 2009 shooting spree at Fort Hood, Texas; the execution remains scheduled to proceed by firing squad.

Immediate families of victims may still witness the execution in person, while President Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday that many "well meaning people would rather not watch him die" through streaming.

In his Truth Social post, Trump cited FBI communications between Hasan and Yemeni-American cleric Anwar al-Awlaki during President Barack Obama administration, though investigators previously concluded those emails posed no threat.
title: Trump, after bipartisan backlash, says Pentagon won't livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter

summary: On Wednesday, October 14, 2026, the Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027, affecting more than 76 million Americans. This annual adjustment aims to help beneficiaries manage rising prices for essential goods and services.

The 3.6% figure derives from the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers , which tracked average price changes from July through September 2026. This metric measures inflation across a basket of goods purchased by workers.

Retirees will receive an average monthly payment increase of $75 in 2027. The projected Medicare Part B premium increase of just $6.60 suggests many seniors may retain more of this year's COLA than in recent years.

Senior advocacy groups argue this adjustment fails to restore lost purchasing power. AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan noted that one in five older Americans lacks retirement savings, intensifying financial insecurity amid persistent inflation.

Without legislative reform, the Old Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund faces depletion by 2032. Experts warn this could trigger a 22% payment cut for beneficiaries, a long-standing concern for the system's long-term viability.
title: Social Security Administration announces 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027

The executive order waives specified provisions under Sections 102 through 117 of the law, while Trump directed the Trade Representative to monitor ongoing purchases of Russian energy and report circumstances indicating further action may be needed.

Administration officials stated the waivers serve the national interest of the United States, though the decision faces criticism from lawmakers concerned that easing restrictions could provide revenue to Moscow while the war in Ukraine continues.

Starting Sunday, October 18, 2026, the pay increase takes effect and is backdated to the beginning of the year, providing relief to a demoralized workforce.

summary: On Friday, ExxonMobil reported that soaring refining margins could increase its downstream earnings by $4.5 billion in the third quarter, ahead of full results scheduled for October 30.

Refining margins climbed sharply as the war involving Iran restricted energy exports through the Strait of Hormuz , while Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries pressured global fuel supplies. Exxon's integrated business model balances upstream and downstream operations to capitalize on these disruptions.

Exxon projects about $15.1 billion in adjusted earnings for the quarter, up from $14.7 billion previously. A $1.3 billion headwind from lower liquids prices in the Upstream segment was partially offset by a $300 million benefit from gas price changes and $700 million from divestments.

ExxonMobil Holdings shares closed 2.46% higher at $178.98 on Friday, reaching a new 52-week high. Morgan Stanley raised its price target to $185, while BMO Capital Markets analyst Phillip Jungwirth estimated refining net income could reach $8.5 billion.
Analysts estimate earnings per share of $3.83, up from $1.88 last year, as the company continues its 43-year streak of raising dividends. Full financial results are scheduled for October 30.
title: ExxonMobil signals $4.5 billion refining earnings boost as margins soar

At Nyangezi General Hospital in Congo, health workers reported stockouts of life-saving medications including oxytocin, while midwife Alice Bulambo told Reuters, "It was a donation we received from USAID, and at the moment, there is none."
U.S. authorities extended deadlines for Chemonics deliveries of malaria and HIV items and signed a separate deal with the Global Fund to allow countries to order supplies through its platform.

The US has signed more than 30 bilateral health aid deals requiring co-financing, while the Congolese government aims to take over maternal health responsibilities by next year, Polydor Kabila, coordinator of the universal healthcare programme, said.

summary: Yesterday, the San Francisco-based 9th Circuit Court of Appeals vacated an order allowing California customers to pursue class action claims against Tesla , ruling that individual purchase experiences varied too much to sustain a class action lawsuit.

Plaintiffs contend Tesla misled buyers regarding Full Self-Driving Supervised capabilities, allegedly convincing customers to pay extra for software that does not work. District Judge Rita Lin previously ruled thousands of prospective buyers were likely exposed to these claims.

A three-judge panel, including Circuit Judges Ronald Gould, Jay Bybee, and Daniel Bress, found too many individualized questions regarding what each buyer saw before purchasing. Consequently, thousands of California buyers cannot currently pursue their claims jointly in a single case.

Supporting Tesla, the Chamber of Commerce argued the original ruling threatened to increase costs for businesses, while plaintiffs' lawyers stated the panel failed to appreciate the unique circumstances of the marketing campaign.

While the underlying lawsuit alleging false advertising remains pending, this decision is a procedural win for Tesla; the ruling does not address the merits, so the dispute over technology capabilities continues in court.
title: US appeals court blocks class actions over Tesla's self-driving claims

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the ruling as Trump “loses” and portrays sanctuary protections as immigrant safeguards threatened by an attempted “backdoor around the Tenth Amendment.” Right-leaning accounts instead emphasize states’ rights, saying the government cannot “commandeer locals” or “force” them to assist ICE, while the phrase “illegal immigrants” sharpens a law-and-order tone.
The center largely de-emphasizes these ideological implications, focusing on the judge’s procedural finding that the lawsuit lacked a valid basis and using “sanctuary” in quotes.
The pivotal divide is whether the case represents protection for undocumented immigrants or federal overreach; all sides agree the lawsuit was dismissed and NYC’s limits on cooperation remain.
summary: On Thursday, U.S. District Judge Ramón Reyes dismissed the Trump administration's lawsuit seeking to block New York City's sanctuary laws, finding the federal government lacked legal standing to challenge local policies limiting cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

The Justice Department sued in July 2025, arguing New York City's sanctuary policies violated the U.S. Constitution's Supremacy Clause by barring city agencies from sharing release dates and honoring civil immigration detainers issued by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Judge Reyes wrote that federal law does not require states to assist with immigration enforcement, calling the government's arguments "nothing more than a backdoor around the Tenth Amendment." He noted striking down these provisions would improperly commandeer local personnel and resources.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani hailed the decision as "a victory for New Yorkers," pledging to uphold sanctuary policies and stating these laws allow the city to focus resources on protecting communities without fear of deportation.

The Department of Homeland Security reported that New York City ignored 14,916 immigration detainers between January 2025 and September 2026, while the recent shooting of Oscar Belgal by ICE agents in the Bronx has intensified the enforcement conflict.
title: Judge tosses Trump administration lawsuit over New York City ‘sanctuary’ laws
topic_full: New York State Politics · New York

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the 11 House-rating shifts as “Democratic momentum is surging” and an “expansive battlefield,” stressing opportunities even in districts Trump won by 10 or more points.
Right-Leaning coverage counters with “GOP still favored in 8,” portraying the changes as limited signals rather than likely Democratic victories.
The pivotal divide is whether the ratings indicate a broad partisan realignment or merely increased competitiveness.

Center coverage adds scale—14 Republican-held seats in a broader map—and attributes the climate partly to “Trump’s unpopularity.” All perspectives acknowledge the 11 shifts, reflecting a shared focus on electoral movement amid wider debates over momentum, vulnerability, and Republican resilience.
summary: The Cook Political Report shifted 14 U.S. House seats in 10 states toward Democrats on Saturday, occurring 18 days before the November 3 midterm elections and signaling tighter-than-expected races.

Cook analyst Erin Covey noted Republican troubles are 'particularly pronounced in Midwestern red states,' where districts President Donald Trump won by 10 points or more in 2024 are now 'firmly in play.'

In Florida's 25th District, Republicans spent $14 million against Rep. Jared Moskowitz, while in New York's 21st District, Democrat Blake Gendebien leads Republican Anthony Constantino 46 percent to 42 percent.

Republican National Committee Press Secretary Natalie Baldassarre told Newsweek the party remains "laser-focused on winning," pouring resources into battleground districts to boost candidates and protect President Trump's majority.
The GOP currently holds a 218-214 edge in the House, leaving little margin for error as forecasters including Cook and Fox News have made 152 rating changes favoring Democrats since Labor Day.
title: Cook Political Report shifts 11 House seats away from GOP

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the tragedy through collective heroism, calling an “alert father” and teacher people who “helped save lives,” while right-leaning coverage spotlights individual courage, using “tackled” and “fought” to portray the teacher as a self-reliant defender confronting a “shooter.” The pivotal divide is the father’s role: left coverage elevates his vigilance, whereas center reporting specifies that a parent killed the attacker, alongside the unresolved motive and the special-education setting.
Center language such as “likely” retains caution.

Across perspectives, all emphasize the 16-year-old suspect, four deaths, police accounts, and lifesaving intervention, reflecting shared concern with violence while differing over agency, context, and self-defense.
summary: On Friday, a 16-year-old former student killed four people and wounded two others at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, before a parent intervened and shot the assailant, officials said.
Griffin shot through locked glass doors to enter the campus, firing about 15 rounds in a special needs classroom where he killed three children and a teacher.
A teacher fought the shooter by throwing her cellphone and tackling him, while Kaylub Giamanco, a parent, entered the classroom and shot the gunman, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz reported.
Residents of Bend gathered near the school on Friday to mourn, placing flowers and candles outside yellow crime scene tape, as Krantz stated the bystander's actions "undoubtedly saved people."
Such shootings revive debates over gun laws in the country, where the right to "keep and bear Arms" is protected under the Constitution's Second Amendment.
title: Teacher and armed parent teamed up to stop Oregon school shooter, police say

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the roughly 600-soldier deployment as “mission creep,” a “quietly upping” U.S. footprint, and part of a “long and bloody history” of intervention, stressing strategic risk and regional memory.

Right-Leaning accounts foreground a forceful “anti-cartel campaign,” “fight” against drug trafficking , and joint exercises, though notable doubts about the campaign’s goals complicate that security framing.
Center coverage de-emphasizes historical critique while highlighting sovereignty concerns and operational details.
The pivotal divide is whether Panama—and potentially Colombia and Honduras—represents limited training or expanding intervention.
All perspectives acknowledge the 10th Mountain Division deployment, regional exercises, and anti-narcotics purpose, reflecting broader clashes over militarism, sovereignty, and U.S. power.
summary: The United States is deploying a 600-soldier battalion from the 10th Mountain Division, based at Fort Drum, N.Y., to Panama for jungle training, with follow-on rotations planned for Colombia and Honduras.
Gen. Joseph A. Ryan, commander of U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Command, described the move earlier this week as a reorientation toward a region that for decades was not a military priority.

Legal analysts warn against extending military strikes inland, citing civilian casualties risks; the Pentagon previously conducted 71 attacks on boats, killing at least 239 people it says were involved in trafficking, though the administration has presented no evidence.

Stretched by the war with Iran, U.S. military capacity faces strain, officials warned, risking escalation if armed groups strike American troops and draw forces into a deeper conflict without a clear exit plan.

While these rotations are currently temporary, they could become a permanent feature of U.S. military presence; the administration has built a 19-nation coalition, though only a few countries have formally agreed to joint operations on their soil.
title: Hegseth ramps up US troops in Panama as Pentagon expands war on drug cartels

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds the “anti-Lula political bias” accusation while treating Meta ’s denial as a dispute; right-leaning coverage pivots to allegations that recommendations “favored” Bolsonaro-related content, calling them “clear interference,” while amplifying Meta’s counterclaim of “technical incidents” rather than ideological intent.
The pivotal divide is whether unequal treatment reflects partisan manipulation or system malfunction, alongside differing attention to AI restrictions and campaign effects.
Center coverage adds procedural context, emphasizing the electoral court’s demand for “equal treatment” before the runoff.
Across perspectives, all stress Meta’s denial, the court ruling, and tensions between platform governance, electoral fairness, and Brazil’s ideological polarization.
summary: Meta denied accusations Friday that it acted with political bias during Brazil's presidential campaign, less than a day after the country's electoral court ruled the platform must give equal treatment to incumbent Luiz Lula Silva and opposition candidate Bolsonaro ahead of their Oct. 25 runoff.
Lula Silva's campaign triggered the lawsuit, alleging that Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, used biased algorithms and AI restrictions to favor Bolsonaro.

A study released this week by researchers at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro found Meta allowed at least 1,613 irregular political ads totaling 171 million views and generating roughly 2 million reais in revenue between July and September.
Meta insisted its systems do not distribute content based on political ideology and pledged to ensure a level playing field for all users, emphasizing that rules apply equally to all candidates.

These allegations mirror European cases in Germany and Romania where courts intervened to correct platform imbalances, as Brazil continues efforts to hold Big Tech accountable for electoral transparency.
title: Meta denies accusation of anti-Lula political bias in Brazil after electoral court ruling

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the warning as federal escalation against “heavily Democratic California,” using “fight” and “ongoing tussle” while stressing that voters are merely “suspected” noncitizens and officials “risk prosecution,” evoking due-process concerns.

Right-Leaning coverage presents a forceful election-integrity intervention: “stark warning,” “warning shot,” and “bitter voting showdown” amplify urgency, while the reported lawsuit involving 20,000 suspected voters supplies numerical weight.
Center coverage remains procedural, foregrounding attribution and conditional language.
The pivotal divide is whether the action signifies intimidation and partisan conflict or necessary deterrence against illegal voting.
All perspectives emphasize the DOJ warning, possible criminal investigation, and the looming election, reflecting broader federal-state and election-security tensions.
summary: On Friday, the Justice Department warned California election officials that processing ballots from individuals flagged as suspected noncitizens could lead to criminal prosecution, following a federal lawsuit filed Thursday.

The Trump administration's aggressive hunt for noncitizen voters has escalated tensions with California ahead of next month's midterm election, after previously claiming as many as 250,000 noncitizens were registered across four states.

Federal authorities provided a list of 20,000 names on a password-protected thumb drive, demanding a 48-hour review; however, California Secretary of State Shirley Weber stated the administration provided no evidence to support the claims.

UCLA law professor Rick Hasen called the threats "deplorable," noting they pressure officials during an ongoing election, while potential cases in Los Angeles would be handled by federal prosecutor Bill Essayli.
The Justice Department has charged about 90 individuals for election misconduct this year, including 50 alleged noncitizen voters, amid over 23 million registered voters statewide in California.
title: California officials who process ballots from suspected noncitizens risk prosecution, US warns

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds alleged “torture,” “abuse,” “violence suffered,” and testimony from about 50 activists, extending scrutiny up Israel ’s chain of command.
Center coverage stresses the accusations’ “very heavy” breadth—“assault,” kidnapping, robbery, injury, and damage—while retaining procedural framing.

Right-Leaning coverage highlights the inquiry’s expansion from “far-right” minister Itamar Ben-Gvir to Israel Katz and other officials, using the more neutral “treatment” and cautioning that allegations are not findings of guilt.
The key divide is whether to spotlight alleged human-rights abuses or institutional and legal process.
All perspectives report Rome’s investigation, tied to two flotilla missions and senior Israeli authorities.
summary: Italian prosecutors announced on Friday an expanded investigation into Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz and senior military, police, and prison officials over treatment of Gaza flotilla activists during missions in 2025 and 2026.

Investigators launched the probe after receiving complaints from 50 Italian citizens who were detained by Israeli authorities during two Global Sumud Flotilla missions spanning September to October 2025 and April to May 2026.

Allegations include torture, kidnapping, beatings, and death threats, with prosecutors naming 12 senior Israeli military, police, and prison officials as suspects, including military chief Eyal Zamir.
Itamar Ben-Gvir, previously targeted by the investigation, dismissed the probe, stating he would "continue to stand proudly alongside our fighters."
Under Italian law, crimes committed abroad against Italian citizens can be prosecuted in Rome; being under investigation does not imply guilt or automatically lead to trial.
title: Italy names senior Israelis, Katz in probe over Gaza flotilla activists

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds Palestinian dispossession and Israeli responsibility, using phrases such as “abandoned morality,” “crossed the line,” and “took Palestinian land” to portray military superiority as incapable of delivering security.

Right-Leaning coverage reframes the same remarks as an assault on Jewish history and Israel ’s legitimacy, calling Obama “anti-Semitic,” “under fire,” or dismissive of a “3,000-year” connection, while emphasizing Israel’s “right to defend itself” and Netanyahu’s “ancestral homeland” claim.

Center coverage briefly presents both positions with attributed language like “ceded moral ground.” The pivotal divide is whether the episode signifies occupation and moral failure or historical erasure and threatened self-defense; all perspectives agree Obama criticized Israel, Netanyahu rebutted him, and the remarks sparked controversy.
summary: On Tuesday, former President Barack Obama spoke at the O2 arena in Belfast, Northern Ireland, arguing that Israel's founding involved "injustice" against Palestinians and criticizing the government's reliance on military force.
Speaking with journalist Susan McKay, Obama acknowledged Jewish persecution in Europe while asserting that Israel's establishment involved taking land and being "excessive."
Critics accused the former president of distorting history, arguing he overlooked more than 3,000 years of Jewish ties to the Land of Israel and minimized continuous Jewish presence in the region.

Obama warned that Israel has "ceded moral ground" by prioritizing military solutions, arguing the citizenry must "rethink, reimagine" how to coexist with Palestinians rather than relying on walls and force.

Regarding the path forward, Obama stated Palestinians must abandon expectations of military victory and pursue "nonviolent strategies," acknowledging that lasting peace requires significant diplomatic effort and creative engagement.
title: Israel 'Took the Land' From Palestinians, Has 'Ceded Moral Ground,' Obama Tells Belfast Crowd

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the allegations as an escalating human-rights crisis, emphasizing a “surge,” “severely injuring,” 21 documented cases, and the Prison Service’s dismissal as a “smear campaign.” Center coverage retains attribution through “report,” but broadens the issue into “harsh treatment” and de-emphasizes case-specific evidence.

Right-Leaning coverage avoids “surge” and instead foregrounds graphic consequences—surgery, a fractured shin, and testicle removal—while portraying prisoners as “severely injured.” The pivotal divide is whether to stress systemic escalation, historical conditions, or individual harm, alongside whether official denial merits attention.

All perspectives nevertheless highlight close-range rubber-bullet shootings, serious injuries, and rights-group allegations, reflecting the conflict’s broader ideological divide over Israeli security and Palestinian rights.
summary: Israeli human rights groups have documented 22 cases of inmates shot with rubber bullets, reporting a surge in the practice that has become routine violence in prisons. One of the 22 detainees is Israeli; the rest are Palestinian.

Conditions in Israeli prisons deteriorated dramatically since the war in Gaza began more than three years ago. Following the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks, authorities rounded up thousands of Palestinians, doubling the prison population to more than 9,000, according to Hamoked.

Medical records from Soroka document a 45-year-old inmate whose testicle was "completely crushed" by a rubber bullet, requiring surgical removal. Other detainees report being shot at point-blank range in cells, with several stating they received no medical treatment for resulting injuries.

Under Israel's prison regulations, guards may only use weapons when facing imminent risk, said Sari Bashi, executive director of the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel. However, the prison service's legal adviser defended the use of rubber bullets as "measured" and "appropriate."

Muhannad Abu Ghosh, director of the prisoners and detainees division at Physicians for Human Rights Israel, warned the practice is "becoming another routine form of violence." Rights groups urge the prison service to end behavior they call widespread and unlawful.
title: Israeli rights groups report a surge of Palestinian inmates being shot with rubber bullets
